Snapshot/iterator, fire-and-forget, on-trigger select, subquery IN, and output-rate-limit (every-events, every-time, snapshot) all dedup. Batch-window join distinct (BatchWindowJoin) works: join tuple identity is lineage-keyed, so a batch rollover that replaces same-content rows still emits the full old/new pair the way Esper composes join results per arriving or departing event, while rebuilt historical and method sides keep their previous lineage on equal content and net out; distinct then collapses each batch to first-seen key order. Every-distinct pattern joins (JoinPatternOne/Two) work: each every-distinct leg inside the followed-by stays resident, so a captured fooA branch pairs with every later distinct wooA and each new distinct fooA starts another branch (Java probe: JoinPatternOne fires exactly one batch of six rows {E1,E1},{E1,E2},{E2,E2},{E1,E3},{E2,E3},{E3,E3}; JoinPatternTwo delivers the ordered {E1,E2},{E1,E3} pair). The Go pattern engine fans out a new sequence branch per left-leg firing, re-arms a repeating right leg with its fired flag reset while keeping its distinct keyspace, gates sequence advancement on fresh every-leg completions (the retained done flag alone no longer re-advances), and treats such completions as non-permanent so the pattern keeps producing until the within deadline. The SupportSubscriberMRD multi-row Object[][] subscriber surface (OBSERVEROPS) is asserted through the listener ResultBatch model; Go has no separate subscriber SPI.

Go inserts through OnEvent(...).InsertIntoNamedWindow trigger plans as the established equivalent of EPL insert-into select statements, and reads iterator state with NamedWindow.Snapshot in retention order. FirstEventWindowSpec retention is newly honored by named windows: a dropped firstevent insert produces no listener callback at all. Sort windows iterate in sort order with newer equal-key events before older ones (reverseSortedEqualRuns), and an event sorting beyond the retained size of a full window is inserted and removed in the same delta (IR pair with itself). Unique snapshot order follows first-seen key order where Esper asserts any-order. Time views run on a virtual clock via Engine.AdvanceTime: #time expires exactly at insert-time plus the period; firsttime admits only while the oldest retained event is younger than the period and never timer-expires; time_batch accumulates silently, delivers the completed batch as new data at the anchored boundary and as old data at the following boundary (one callback carries both when both exist), with silent deletes of unflushed events and a boundary schedule that slides by the period even across empty batches. length_batch shares the time_batch completed-batch state machine with a size trigger: accumulation and unflushed deletes are silent, each completed batch is one new-data delivery and leaves as old data when the next batch completes; firstlength drops inserts beyond the size silently until deletes free a slot; time_accum delivers inserts immediately and expires all retained events together at the newest retained event plus the period, re-anchoring when the newest event is deleted. ext_timed(value, period) slides with arriving event timestamps: each event expires when the newest timestamp seen reaches its timestamp plus the period, expiries ride in the same delta as the triggering insert and both the window listener and the irstream consumer observe the IR pair. ext_timed_batch anchors boundaries at the epoch reference, accumulates silently, fires old data for deletes of accumulated events, and an arriving event whose timestamp crosses the next boundary flushes the accumulated batch as new data and the previously completed batch as old data. time_order keeps events sorted by their external timestamp, expires them under the engine clock at timestamp plus the period, and an arrival whose external timestamp is already expired passes straight through as an IR pair with itself. time_length_batch shares the time_batch anchored rollover with an additional size trigger, silent accumulation and silent unflushed deletes, and an all-empty rollover disarms the schedule until the next insert re-anchors it (Esper re-anchoring). #groupwin(key)#length(size) retains the newest size events per group with the flat iterator in insertion order, expelling the oldest events of an over-full group as old data in the triggering insert delta; #groupwin(key)#time_batch(duration) shares the anchored time_batch rollover and silent accumulation/deletes, delivering the completed batch with events grouped by key in first-seen group order. The four EPL on-delete alias variants (as on the trigger stream, on the window, both or neither) collapse into one Go chain construction because typed trigger/window fields make stream aliases unnecessary; the shared tryCreateWindow consumer matrix (doubling projection, per-key grouped sum with irstream null-prior IR pairs, value >= 10 filter) is asserted against one Go window. Go delete-trigger statements deliver deleted window events as the old data of the trigger batch while Esper delivers them as the new data of the on-delete statement; both fire exactly when rows matched (the Java no-op assertListenerInvoked is satisfied by the lingering first-delete invocation), so invocation counts are asserted instead of trigger payloads. Grouped irstream aggregates now emit the Esper null-prior old row on group creation (group-by columns populated, aggregate columns null). Two insert-into statements into the same window deliver one window delta each (two listener invocations per source event) and the consumer observes both rows flattened. A filtered irstream consumer applies its filter to new and old events, so a unique replacement whose incoming event fails the filter delivers only the old row. The timetolive retention expression is an epoch-millis Func2 over CurrentTime() plus the per-event longPrimitive field, and the whole-bean insert is an on-merge trigger whose never-matching condition (Literal(false)) with CopyMatchingFields mirrors 'on SupportBean merge MyWindow insert select *'. Invalid-matrix boundaries that Esper reports at compile/deploy time surface at Go register/build time: a groupwin child that is not a data window view fails NewNamedWindowDefinition (ErrorInvalidRule), deleting from an undeclared window fails Build (ErrorUnknownName), a duplicate window name fails registration (ErrorDependency, matching Esper's deploy-time precondition), and a data window declared onto a named-window consumer fails Build (ErrorInvalidRule, groupwin exempt as in Esper). EPL-text-only invalid cases (create window without any view, on-demand update EPL, istream FAF update, model-after unresolved property) are unconstructible in the Go API because CreateNamedWindow takes an explicit schema and defaults retention to keep-all, and update triggers are typed assignments rather than on-demand EPL text. Late-deployed consumers attach to the current named-window state at Go Deploy time (seedNamedWindowConsumerLocked replays retained rows without emitting listener batches), matching Esper's statement-start preload; Esper skips the preload for batching windows (time_batch/length_batch/time_length_batch/firsttime/ext_timed_batch/expression_batch) and so does Go (namedWindowRetentionIsBatch). Esper's #uni(value) on a named-window consumer is the univariate statistics derived view (not the #unique data window), selected in Go as UnivariateStatistics(field).Average() inside an ungrouped Aggregate projection. Esper prior(N, x) maps to Go Prior(N-1, x) with the consumer statement tracking the named-window arrival history per prior conventions. Esper derives a distinct event type for the create-window select columns; the Go port registers a distinct struct for that window schema because re-registering the SupportBean struct under the window schema name would re-point the Go-type to event-type index and misroute bean sends. Multi-key grouped retention is constructed with GroupWindowKeys([]Expr{...}, inner), generalizing GroupWindow(key, inner); per-key state pairs compose one group identity while single-key behavior is unchanged. Pattern statements consuming a named window observe its insert stream; Esper parses every a=W(k1) or a=W(k2) with the every on the first branch only, so a permanent completion of the second branch quits the whole or-expression including the every sibling (EvalOrStateNode isQuitted propagation). The Go pattern runtime mirrors this with patternCompletionPermanent and a quit marker on the or progress; the same fix makes root patterns without every single-fire (plain filter/sequence/and completions quiesce the statement instead of starting a fresh match per event), which rewrote two Go-native assertions to the Java-probed single-fire behavior (and consume refire expectation, within-expr deadline test re-armed with an explicit every). On-trigger inserts against named windows run preemptively in both engines: the Go dispatch loop queues routed insert-into-stream events until every statement has processed the current event, so a cascaded on-select observes window mutations from sibling triggers regardless of declaration order. The stream-target form is a select trigger with RouteTo (TriggerQuery.Query now carries routeTarget and validateRoute admits select triggers), the window-target form is InsertIntoNamedWindowFrom(target, source, assignments) evaluating NamedWindowField against each retained source row (the ordered-assignment helper is bypassed because it would shadow the source row with a target working row). Java creates the insert-into stream type implicitly from the select columns; Go registers the map schema explicitly, matching the established explicit-schema convention. Intersection view stacks (IntersectWindows(LengthWindow(2), Unique(intPrimitive))) now model Esper IntersectDefaultView/IntersectAsymetricView named-window semantics: each child view retains independently, the window contents are the intersection of the child contents, an event expelled by any child leaves as old data in the triggering insert delta, and an insert rejected by an asymmetric child (FirstUnique) produces no new data. On-delete removes the window contents from every child view; on-update delivers the original rows as old data and the replacements as new data, recomputing the intersection so child views stay consistent for later inserts (Java-probed Esper 9.0.0 sequences, including the post-update expiry trace). Composite children are validated at definition time (intersection-only, at least two children, keep-all/length/unique child views). InfraDeepSupertypeInsert bean-class hierarchy (SupportOverrideOneA extends One extends Base, every level overriding getVal() so the single Esper property val carries the most-derived valOneA value) is modeled with flat Go structs exposing only the Esper-visible val property; the valOne/valBase constructor state has no getter and is invisible to Esper. Go struct schemas cannot inherit parent fields through WithSchemaParent (duplicated struct fields are rejected; schema inheritance covers Map/JSON/ObjectArray), so the deep-supertype window insert is expressed with an explicit SetColumn assignment per the typed chain convention, matching the Java observable behavior (insert succeeds, window iterator val=1a). InfraSelectStreamDotStarInsert (insert into a one-column object-array window select intPrimitive as p0, sb.* as c0) compiles in Esper and silently drops the stream-star column at insert (Java-probed Esper 9.0.0: the object-array row holds p0 only). The Go typed chain deliberately validates insert columns against the window schema, so the undeclared c0 column is a Build-time ErrorUnknownName (approved difference); the expressible p0-only form retains exactly p0, matching the Java runtime observation. InfraBeanBacked runs under the object-array/map/default/Avro representation annotations, but @EventRepresentation is inert for create-window-as-bean-type (every rep asserts BeanEventType with the SupportBean underlying), so one Go pass covers the matrix; window-delivered events carry the window name as their event type through the create listener, a plain consumer statement and the on-update trigger batch, matching the Java assertEvent observations. Esper BeanEventType/EventTypeTypeClass.NAMED_WINDOW metadata and the isStatelessSelect SPI flag have no Go public-API counterparts (type-name plus bean underlying are the asserted proxies). InfraBeanContained (create window as (bean SupportBean_S0), insert select bean.* as bean) is modeled with a Go struct window schema whose single bean field carries the whole SupportBean_S0 underlying via EventValue[T](), and the bean.p00 fragment navigation works through the nested struct path; Esper runs the object-array/map/default representations for the composite type (Go keeps its single struct representation) and rejects the Avro form at compile time because a bean property has no Avro mapping, while Go Avro schemas are record-field declarations normalized at ingestion (both recorded as differences). InfraBeanSchemaBacked (create schema ABC as SupportBean.class) models the class-alias event type with a distinct Go struct carrying the same fields: one event type per Go struct matches Esper type identity (SupportBean sends never route to the ABC alias consumer), and the FAF row off the ABC-backed window carries the window-named event type; registering the same Go struct under a second schema name would re-point the Go-type index and misroute sends (the documented hazard), so the alias keeps its own struct.

Go update-istream mirrors Esper's InternalEventRouter copy-on-write preprocessing (Java-probed: the source statement's listeners observe the original event, the update listener receives new=updated-copy/old=original, downstream consumers observe the copy and the original underlying is never mutated). Every set expression evaluates against the pre-update event, so intBoxed=intPrimitive reads the original value even when intPrimitive is assigned earlier. Listener batches follow Go deployment order (Insert, Update, Select) while Esper's router preprocessing invokes the update callback before the insert statement's own listeners; per-statement batch contents are identical. A non-boolean where clause is compile-time impossible in the typed Go builder (Where takes Expression[bool]). Update statements preprocess the event ahead of every consumer in the dispatch cycle regardless of deployment order (orderUpdateStatementsFirst), matching the router-time application probed in Java when update_2 deploys after s0; chained updates observe the prior copy. Null writes to non-nullable properties are skipped after boxed-nil normalization while the insert/remove pair still fires, and boxed values widen numerically towards pointer targets (int to long). The update statement iterator surface (Esper: empty) and subscriber SPI are not asserted (no Go counterparts). Priority annotation parity: update entries on one stream apply in ascending @Priority order so the highest priority assignment wins, ties fall back to the drop entry first then deployment order, and each update's where clause and insert/remove pair observe the running copy left by the previous update; unprioritized updates apply in deployment order with the last assignment winning. @Drop removes the event from the dispatch cycle entirely (the drop statement itself delivers no batch); if a drop follows an earlier matching update, the earlier update's already-queued listener batch is still delivered (Esper suppresses it, an edge unobservable in this suite). The Go parity tests exercise the map representation of MyStream where Esper loops every EventRepresentationChoice; the routed copy-on-write semantics are representation-independent. Nested map-entry and array-element writes (props('abc')=1, myarray[2]=10) clone the target container before writing so the original event's nested map/slice is never mutated; the old IR pair keeps referencing the original containers. A null container, null index or null key skips the write silently; an out-of-range index fails the statement with Esper's update-istream diagnostic text ('Array length 3 less than index 10 for property 'doublearray''); a null rhs writes the zero value into nilable element types and is skipped otherwise. The duplicate-assignment rule keys on the full target identity (column plus index/key description) so distinct indexes or keys on one property are allowed. The Go parity tests exercise the bean and map representations once where Esper loops every EventRepresentationChoice; on-trigger map-entry assignments are Build-rejected pending the named-window slice. On-trigger updates now share the nested-write surface: map-entry assignments are enabled for on-trigger actions (table, named-window, merge) with the update-istream clone-on-write semantics. Esper's out-of-range behavior is target-dependent (source-verified): the plain named-window on-trigger update skips an out-of-range indexed write silently (NWSetMapProps), so the Go updateWhere path passes lenientIndexBounds, while table updates, merge actions, FAF updates and update-istream fail with Esper's diagnostic text (InfraNWTableOnMerge.InfraSetArrayElementWithIndexInvalid is the table oracle). Boxed element writes widen and rebox numerics (int literal to *float64) through coerceUpdateSetValue, and the builder accepts numeric-to-boxed-numeric element assignments. Esper's compile-time invalid message texts differ from Go's typed-builder diagnostics while rejecting the same statement shapes. NWSetMapProps' SERDEREQUIRED flag (HA serde round-trip) has no Go counterpart. Representation and model-surface executions are covered by equivalent-representation parity with approved differences: SODA's EPStatementObjectModel/toEPL/eplToModel model API and the update's optional stream alias have no counterpart in Go's immutable typed chain plans (runtime update-with-where shape asserted on the map rep); XMLEvent's XML DOM representation has no Go counterpart (insert-with-literal-columns plus update asserted on the map rep); WrappedObject's bean-fragment-plus-extra-columns wrapping is asserted on the equivalent flat implicit stream across three update shapes and undeploy/redeploy boundaries; CopyMethod's user copy method is unnecessary in Go where structs always copy field-wise; Expression's inlined_class Helper.swap is JVM-only and the set-with-method-call form has no Go counterpart, while the observable map swap falls out of Go's all-set-expressions-evaluate-pre-update rule with two plain assignments. Subquery set and where expressions are enabled: the update dispatch binds EvalContext.Engine for snapshot access and EvalContext.OuterEvent to the pre-update event so correlated subqueries resolve against the arriving event (Esper's ABCStreamSQ.theString / as-mystream alias scope); the optional stream alias itself has no Go counterpart and the alias redeploy boundary is mirrored with a fresh identical plan. A null scalar subquery result writes null into nullable properties and skips the write on non-nullable ones (existing rules), matching Esper's logged-error-keep-value primitive behavior. Esper's scalar grouped subselect (null on zero or multiple groups, multikey array group keys) is surfaced through the new SubqueryGroupScalar expression. Subqueries remain Build-rejected inside array-index and map-key assignment expressions. Plain update-set assignments are now type-validated at Build time: the expression type must be assignable or widen numerically towards the property type (Esper rejects narrowing assignments such as Long to int; Go ranks int below int64 to mirror Esper int/long even though both are 64-bit here), and a null literal to a non-nullable property is a compile-time rejection (Esper nullable type mismatch) while expression-produced nulls keep the runtime skip behavior. Enumeration lambdas work in update where clauses (EnumAnyOf with element-is-not-null). Esper-only rejection classes are approved differences: read-only bean properties (Go struct schema fields are always writable), the non-copyable bean rejection (all Go structs copy field-wise), XML event write access (no XML representation) and unprefixed outer references in correlated subqueries (Go correlation is always explicit through OuterField). An update-istream whose target is a named window binds to the window insert path (Esper's update strategy): Go preprocesses every offered event copy-on-write inside the named-window insert so the window contents, window listeners, select/on-select/on-insert consumers and the update statement's own IR pair all observe the updated copy, while the feeding insert or on-trigger statement publishes the pre-update row; the window-targeted update never consumes plain stream events nor the window delta as a subscriber, and priority-ordered chained updates observe the running copy. Esper's milestone serde checkpoints have no Go counterpart. The bean class hierarchy of the inheritance execution (create schema ... as <class> with interface and subclass targeting) is modeled with map schemas and WithSchemaParent chains because bean class inheritance has no Go counterpart; supertype acceptance for both update targets and select-from-supertype consumers rides the transitive schema-parent walk, and @Priority orders updates across the hierarchy. Esper's routeEventMap/routeEventBean from a listener map to Engine.Route, a reentrant Send from the listener callback (listeners dispatch after the engine lock is released); routed events pass through update-istream preprocessing and @Drop identically for map and bean representations, while Esper's route-queue timing inside the current unit of work is not separately asserted (Go routes process synchronously inside the listener callback before the outer send returns).
remaining: update-istream on named-window targets (EPLOtherUpdateNamedWindow)

cases.difference: Go expresses unary minus with the typed analyzable Negate constructor rather than EPL prefix syntax. The parity test covers both an int event property and a float64 runtime variable, verifies the projected -10/-1.0 values, and confirms expression evaluation does not mutate the variable.

Go exposes SplitFirst and SplitAll on a typed TriggerStream, with explicit SplitInto/SplitIntoWhen branches and pre-registered target schemas instead of EPL/SODA split clauses. SplitFrom(source).Into/IntoWhen adds a branch-local fluent source derived from the on-event root; source/filter/contained-event chains are evaluated branch-first so output-all preserves Begin/body/End route ordering, output-first selects the first branch producing rows, and one selected contained branch may emit multiple rows. SplitFirst stops after the first true branch, SplitAll emits every true branch, an unconditional final branch is the default, and when no branch matches the split statement emits the original source event. Wildcard branches preserve source fields through target-schema projection; named projections evaluate against the source event and may read ContainedParentField/ContainedParentEvent. A SplitInto target may name either a registered event type or a Named Window. Named Window targets are inserted immediately while ordinary stream routes remain queued, so a later-declared window branch is visible to an earlier-declared ordinary route's on-select cascade; map, ObjectArray, Avro, JSON and typed JSON target representations preserve their schema kind. Branch predicates and projections share the statement subquery registry: the scalar lastevent case preserves Null before SupportBean_S0 arrives and selects p00/p01 after it, while SubqueryGroupScalar over []int keys returns one-group sums and Null for multiple groups without requiring Go-comparable array keys. The FromClause documentation flow routes Begin, Item and End events through one queue, allowing an initiated-terminated context to emit the item count at termination. A context-bound single insert projects ContextID, the ContextInitiatingEvent underlying pointer and the current trigger underlying pointer without losing object identity. The builder rejects missing branches, unknown targets, unrelated/stateful branch sources, non-bool conditions and direct aggregate projections; aggregate expressions remain valid inside a subquery boundary. SODA/model round-trips are intentionally absent and are represented by the immutable fluent Plan.

Go constructs all seven basic statements with typed fluent builders rather than EPL text. StatementName is stable deployment metadata and covers the only annotation value asserted by the Java execution; Java Tag/Priority/Drop annotation-array reflection is not copied onto ordinary select statements. Wildcard select and length-window IR results preserve underlying pointer identity, CountAll emits 1/2/3, the field filter and named projection match Java, and the one-shot timer example uses TimerAt at the equivalent virtual-clock deadline because Go's TimerInterval builder is intentionally recurring.

Go exposes SubscribeWithReplay(ctx, Listener) instead of addListenerWithReplay(UpdateListener). The first synchronous callback always carries the current Snapshot view, including one empty ResultBatch for an empty statement; live events arriving or sent reentrantly during replay are buffered and delivered afterwards as separate batches. Undeploy leaves retained Statement metadata readable while State reports StatementDestroyed and Snapshot, selector Snapshot, Subscribe, SubscribeWithReplay, Stop and Start all return ErrorState. Java iterator and safeIterator share Go's immutable Snapshot boundary; Java setSubscriber overloads are intentionally represented by the typed Listener API rather than duplicated as a reflective subscriber SPI.

Go exposes Engine.SetUnmatchedListener(UnmatchedListener); nil disables delivery. The callback runs after the engine transaction lock is released, so it can deploy a fluent Plan and affect the next event. Matching is based on active input stream filters and deliberately ignores post-input having/output suppression. Unconsumed insert-into routes are reported as their derived Event while an undeployed source statement makes the original external event unmatched with underlying pointer identity preserved. The Java source labels its final insert-into step as a restart without an explicit deploy call; Go expresses that lifecycle transition explicitly by redeploying the immutable plan.

Go statement listeners run after the engine transaction lock is released, so the trigger callback can synchronously inject six representation-specific events with Engine.Route, SendXML and JSONSender.Route; each consumer receives exactly one ident=xy event. Java deploys the seven statements as one EPL module while Go deploys one immutable fluent Plan per statement. Java's preconfigured XML type maps an ident attribute; the Go XML schema test uses its declared ident child element, preserving the same public property value without an EPL/XML configuration layer.

Go exposes AdvanceTimeSpan(ctx, target, optionalResolution), NextScheduledTime and StatementNearestSchedules as typed time.Time APIs. Exact span advancement visits each due instant and therefore preserves one listener batch at 1500/3000/4500/6000/7500/9000/10500 milliseconds. Resolution-based advancement samples in fixed steps; overdue recurring timers fire at the sampled clock and re-anchor there, producing 12100 and 13700 milliseconds for Java's 200-millisecond case. Java timer:interval without every is one-shot, while Go TimerInterval is deliberately recurring, so nearest-schedule parity uses equivalent TimerAt nodes, including TimerAt(3s).And(TimerAt(4s)). Deployment IDs remain explicit in the returned per-statement schedule records.

Java's invalid aggregation function throws RuntimeException from enter and the no-handler regression expects sendEventBean to throw EPException. Go registers the equivalent stateful aggregate by stable name and treats a panic from user-owned factory/state evaluation as an extension-boundary failure: Engine.SendEvent returns ErrorState containing plugin myinvalidagg, statement ABCName and Sample exception. Only the typed aggregate-plugin panic marker is recovered; unrelated runtime panics are rethrown. Java's separately invoked configuration scenarios for duplicated exception-handler factories and ExceptionHandlerContext callbacks are not runtime inventory executions and remain an explicit follow-up rather than being claimed by this case.

Java configurationTransient is represented by immutable named Engine services installed with WithRuntimeService and read from a listener closure. Java statement-selection filter strings are replaced by typed StatementPredicate builders over name, deployment id and canonical Plan, with ordered snapshot traversal outside the engine lock. Java's anonymous BeanEventType service maps to StructSchema without catalog registration. Reflective EPL/module/expression parsing maps to ordinary typed Environment.Build, ExecuteFireAndForget, Deploy, Statement.Snapshot and expression constructors; Plan.Canonical supplies the inspectable model instead of EPL-to-SODA or module text parsing.

Java produces distinct EPCompiled artifact kinds for module EPL and fire-and-forget queries and rejects using one through the other's runtime service. Go deliberately has one immutable typed logical Plan with no text compiler mode bit; the same read-only named-window Plan is valid for ExecuteFireAndForget and Deploy, and both return the same E1 snapshot. This removes an artifact-category misuse rather than weakening query validation, so the Java exception shape is not reproduced.

Java disables its internal timer thread, enables runtime lock-activity logging, sends one SupportBean to a count(*) statement and only asserts that the safe iterator returns c0=1; it does not assert logger text. Go already uses an explicit virtual clock with no internal timer thread by default. WithLockActivityTracing therefore enables an opt-in, bounded in-memory trace of the Engine transaction mutex instead of writing process-global logs. The detached trace records monotonic attempt/acquired/released transitions, supports clear without resetting sequence, and the parity test verifies balanced activity around deploy, send, snapshot and undeploy together with c0=1.

Go exposes StatementPriority and StatementDrop as typed QueryOptions instead of Java annotations. Ordinary continuous dispatch is sorted by descending priority; at equal priority drop statements run first and otherwise deployment order is stable. A drop statement preempts only after it produces a result, and its own listener batch and routes remain visible. The same ordering applies to external and internal routed events, virtual-clock timers, direct and statement-fed named-window deltas, with undeploy/redeploy recomputing the active order. Management traversal deliberately remains deployment ordered. Update-istream retains its separate ascending UpdatePriority/UpdateDrop preprocessing contract, and Build rejects mixing the two option families. Named-window parity uses the same last-event window, typed insert trigger and on-window select shape as Java; Go sends the source by explicit registered name when the same struct also represents ABCStream.

Java exposes the runtime instance ReentrantReadWriteLock and this execution only obtains and releases its writeLock around an administrative action. Go exposes WithRuntimeWriteLock(ctx, action) instead of the raw mutex: the callback runs under the same Engine transaction boundary used by send, deploy, time and state mutation, the lock is always released with defer, nil actions and destroyed engines return structured errors, and callers cannot accidentally retain the lock handle. The parity test proves a concurrent SendEvent cannot complete until the callback releases the lock, then observes c0=1. Go's mutex is intentionally non-reentrant and the callback contract forbids calling another lock-taking Engine method.

Go assembles the solution with typed UniqueBy, TimeWindow, GroupBy, IntoTable, KeepAll Named Window and TimerCron plans. Listener callbacks connect the materialized count statement and minute maintenance statement to situation-window mutations and typed OutputAlerts sends, replacing Java's multi-statement EPL module while retaining rule boundaries and reentrant Engine calls outside the transaction lock. ObjectArray PortScanEvent input, 20 unique ports, 30-second contributor retention, first-only DETECTED, minute UPDATE, UPDATE-before-DONE ordering below count 10 and the 16-hour EXPIRED branch are implemented. The three Java executions assert DETECTED=20, sustained UPDATE=20 after refreshes at 29/59 seconds, and final DONE=0 after expiry; the Go tests assert the same public sequence and contributor-derived detection count.

Go replaces EPL @-annotation text, Java imports/class loading and reflection proxies with typed fluent options and immutable value contracts. StatementDescription, StatementTag, WithStatementHints and StatementNoLock expose built-ins; custom definitions validate required/defaulted attributes, exact Go types, duplicate/unknown fields, nil arrays/elements, nested definition identity, annotation arrays, named string enums and reflect.Type class values. Statement and Query return detached metadata snapshots, schema annotations survive registration and enter Plan identity, and a schema-annotated map event still flows through the normal runtime. Case-insensitive ParseAnnotationStringEnum replaces annotation-specific enum imports. Java EPL/SODA formatting, parser syntax categories, annotation proxy equals/hashCode/toString and raw class names are intentionally not reproduced. NoLock is exposed as an instruction while Go retains its Engine-wide serialized transaction boundary; rule-specific semantic controls remain explicit fluent methods rather than being inferred from metadata.

Go represents a Java compiled module as an ordered []Plan passed to Engine.DeployPlans. Explicit names retain declaration order; unnamed plans receive stmt-0, stmt-1 and so on. WithDeploymentStatementNameResolver receives the immutable Plan, original name and index before the Engine lock, and duplicate or blank resolved names abort before any statement becomes visible. Statement names are unique only inside one Deployment: Engine now indexes active statements by stable statement ID, so separate deployments may both contain name 'a', both dispatch, and undeploying one leaves the other active. Deployment.Statement resolves names without global ambiguity. Java EPCompiled module bytecode and its exact EPDeployException wording are not reproduced; typed plans, structured errors and callback errors are the Go replacement.

Go replaces reflective subscriber objects, named methods, overload selection, static update methods and update/updateRStream footprint matching with one explicit Subscriber callback receiving immutable SubscriberUpdate and SubscriberRow values. Rows expose ordered projection Values, Map, Get and wildcard Underlying; join source Event values bind to their underlying Go values. SetSubscriber replaces or removes the single observer, subscribers coexist with listeners, undeploy clears them, and DisallowSubscriber enters canonical Plan identity. Returned errors and panics are isolated from Send/Route, surfaced through SetSubscriberErrorHandler and do not block listeners or sinks. Go listeners retain their existing fail-fast error contract. Variable-set triggers now emit one assignment row; named-window delete remains an old-stream row under the common ResultBatch model. Registered named windows are catalog objects rather than Java create-window EPStatement instances. Performance executions assert deterministic 1,000-event delivery/no-observer behavior without copying machine-specific one-second thresholds.

Go keeps synchronous Send, Route and AdvanceTime semantics stable and enables concurrency explicitly with WithInboundWorkers, WithOutboundWorkers, WithRouteWorkers and WithTimerWorkers. SendAsync/representation variants, RouteAsync and AdvanceTimeAsync return reusable AsyncTask handles; WaitAsync provides a transitive idle barrier and ThreadingStats exposes workers, queue, in-flight, accepted, completed and dropped counts. Inbound coverage includes map, struct, XML, ObjectArray and JSON plus asynchronous structured-error reporting. Outbound delivery queues the complete subscriber/listener/sink batch and reports asynchronous callback errors through SetThreadingErrorHandler. Engine.Close stops admission, cancels queued work, resolves every task and waits for workers before undeploying. The Engine transaction lock still serializes statement state, so route/timer workers move a complete runtime cycle off the caller instead of mutating 100 statements concurrently. Explicit virtual time replaces Java's optional internal timer thread; tests use blocking gates and exact delivery counts instead of machine-specific sub-100ms thresholds or internal executor-class inspection.

Go expresses one Java compiled module as an ordered DeployPlans call and two Java compiler-path modules as separate immutable Plan deployments over an explicitly registered public derived-stream schema. The same-deployment producer/filtered consumer preserves E1/E4 delivery and E2/E3 suppression; the late consumer does not replay E1 and receives E2-E4. The Table case declares the composite primary key plus BasketIndex in the typed Environment, verifies the selected equality IndexPlan, and joins A/B VWAPrice events to weights 1/2. Java module text, compiler-path access-modifier callbacks and JVM query-plan hooks are not copied. The current continuous Table join preloads its passive Table side at deployment, so this case proves plan selection and observable results rather than a per-event physical index lookup. Deployment-local protected definitions are mapped separately by case.client-multitenancy-protected.

Go uses RegisterModule(name, ProtectedModule()) and Module.Build rather than EPL module text or compiler-path access-modifier callbacks. Module-qualified handles bind Table/Named Window targets, variables, contexts, map event types and declared expressions into immutable Plan identity. Engine deployment atomically materializes the protected runtime catalog, rejects a second active deployment of the same protected module, preserves same logical names in different modules, and removes runtime state on undeploy while another module continues processing. The tests reproduce Java's A/B infra rows, 10/20 timer variables, initiated-context counts, same-name count/sum event schemas and expression values 1/2. Immutable Environment compile artifacts intentionally remain reusable for redeployment.

Go replaces EPL annotations and CompilerPath with RegisterModule plus PrivateModule/PublicModule/ProtectedModule and immutable ModulePath values created by module.Uses(...) or env.Uses(...). Resolution covers event types, variables, contexts, Named Windows, Tables, declared expressions and registered Go scripts; an explicit Uses dependency selects one exporter, while unqualified duplicate public exports and preconfigured/module collisions return ErrorAmbiguous. ModulePath.Build records sorted uses dependencies in Plan canonical identity, Module.Build overrides prior module identity, public Named Window create/insert/select deployments reproduce the Java E1..E4 sums 10/30/45/51, and SendBusRecord admits only public module schemas marked BusEventType. Conflicting visibility options and bus visibility on private/protected modules fail before registration. Java application-inlined classes are migrated to module-local declared expressions or typed Go UDFs; JVM source compilation, classloading, binary paths and exact compiler text are not copied.

Go uses Parameter[T](name) and 1-based ParameterAt[T](position) in analyzable fluent expressions. DeployWithParameters and the new DeployWithPositionalParameters bind one live Plan, while DeployPlans plus WithDeploymentParameterResolver resolves each statement independently and exposes immutable Plan, custom deployment/statement identity, statement metadata, ordered reflect.Type declarations and named ordinals. Named and positional modes cannot mix; positions are contiguous; repeated names require compatible types; missing, extra, wrong-mode and wrong-type values fail before deployment visibility. Parameters are covered in filters, post-window where-equivalents, projections, property access, explicit Cast, Pattern, interface/concrete key inheritance and per-deployment stream Subquery state. Array/slice, nested array and map generic result metadata remains exact reflect.Type. Java primitive/boxed pairs collapse to Go's one int type, untyped parameters use Parameter[any]+Cast, and SODA/text variants share the same immutable Plan.

Java SODA rejects an arbitrary Object constant because the JVM compiler cannot give it a portable bytecode representation and directs callers to substitution parameters. Go does not have that bytecode boundary: Literal(nativeStruct) now contributes deterministic type-and-value identity to the immutable Plan, while Parameter[nativeStruct] remains available for deployment-time binding, and the two plans have distinct hashes. Rejecting a valid native Go literal solely to copy the Java compiler limitation would make the fluent API less Go-like without preserving a runtime semantic property.

The fixed Esper 9.0.0 source declares InstrumentationHelper.ENABLED=false and ASSERTIONENABLED=false. RegressionRunner therefore does not call startTest/endTest, all internal instrumentation branches are compile-time false, and this execution only builds, deploys and undeploys select 1=2 without sending an event or asserting a callback. Go verifies the same observable typed Plan lifecycle and does not copy the dormant JVM-wide static helper, hundreds of q/a callback pairs, bytecode hooks or provider system properties. ClientInstrumentAudit and all MetricsReporting executions are covered by their own mapped capabilities and tests.

Go enables runtime reporting explicitly with WithRuntimeMetrics and publishes immutable RuntimeMetric values through removable typed listeners. The first AdvanceTime establishes the reporting epoch; 10-second periods reproduce Java's 11s and 21s boundaries, cumulative input 1 then 4, deltas 1 then 3, and schedule depth 1 then 0 around a one-shot timer. Like MetricExecEngine, Go captures counts before accounting the metric record itself, so that internal record enters the next period's delta. CurrentRuntimeMetric provides a management snapshot and SetRuntimeMetricsEnabled controls reporting. Go does not inject metrics into the ordinary event schema/catalog or copy JMX/ThreadMXBean per-thread CPU checks; listeners are a management surface. Current schedule depth counts active statements with pending callbacks, which is exact for this execution but not yet a full count of every handle in multi-timer statements. Statement-level metrics remain separate.

Go configures statement metrics with typed StatementMetricsGroup options and delivers immutable StatementMetric values through removable management listeners plus CurrentStatementMetricGroups snapshots. Ordered SQL-LIKE/regexp include-exclude rules, first-match grouping, reportInactive, 6s/7s/8s and dynamically changed intervals, per-statement enable-disable, global schedule pause/resume, reset-on-report, undeploy removal and Named Window input accounting reproduce the five Java executions. Metric listeners are not ordinary statements, so they do not recursively report themselves after application undeploy. Named Window declarations are environment-owned metrics using deploymentId environment; this represents Java create-window statement A/W accounting without introducing EPL declarations. Linux CPUTime uses process CPU time because goroutines may migrate OS threads; non-Linux builds expose zero when no portable sampler exists. WallTime, input, insert-stream and remove-stream counters retain the Java reporting-period contract.

StatementAudit uses typed AuditCategory values and enters immutable Plan identity instead of parsing @Audit text. Bare StatementAudit/Audit enables all 14 Java categories. AuditRecord preserves runtime URI, deployment ID, statement name, context partition ID, category, virtual clock and message; the strict Java STREAM callback is reproduced at runtimeTime=1 with the expected filter/event summary. SubscribeAudit is removable and Engine-local, and callbacks are queued under the transaction lock then delivered outside it so they may safely re-enter Engine APIs. AuditFormatter supports %u/%d/%s/%i/%c/%m/%tutc/%tzone. Dataflow audit is configured on the fluent definition and uses deploymentId environment because Go does not model create-dataflow as an EPL statement; no JVM-global AuditPath logger/callback state is copied.
